name: Persian Miniature
basis: why: flat areas of mineral colour, fine ink outlines, no shadows; how: nine pigments, flat regions, ink outline, gold leaf
note: Miniature pigments are opaque watercolour, which the gouache entry's own history names; gold leaf and ink line are extra operations.

lumenary.blurb: Flat jewel colour with no cast shadows, fine ink outlines, tufts of grass and a gilded frame, as in a page from an illuminated manuscript.

facts.from: Persia and the Timurid, Safavid and Mughal courts
facts.era: Thirteenth to seventeenth century and later
facts.bestOn: Portraits, gardens and scenes with clear shapes

why: A Persian miniature is a small painting made for a book. The painter uses flat areas of mineral colour, draws fine ink outlines, and does not cast shadows. Space is made by stacking things up the page, and meadows are pricked with tufts of grass and small flowers. Its jewel-like colour and its calm, flat world are the opposite of a photograph, and the recipe is easy to follow.
how: Blur the picture (simplify × 1.1 px), make it 25 percent more saturated, and snap each pixel to one of nine pigments by the redmean distance.
Remove specks with a majority filter run twice over a 5 by 5 window.
Draw outlines in dark brown ink where the colour index changes, with a strength of 0.8 × the ink slider.
Use fine parallel hatching for depth where the picture is dark, in place of shadows.
Add gold leaf, tufts of grass and a frame of gold rules and a blue band with gold teardrops on ivory paper.
history: The pigments included lapis lazuli from the mines of Badakhshan, vermilion, malachite green, turmeric yellow and burnished gold leaf. Painting for books flourished at the courts of Tabriz, Herat and Isfahan, with masters such as Kamal ud-Din Behzad in the fifteenth century, and illustrated epics such as the Shahnameh. The Mughal court developed its own school, blending Persian and Indian traditions.
uses: Teaching flat colour, outline and pattern
terms: A small painting, here made for a manuscript.
A deep blue stone ground to make pigment.
Fine parallel lines used to suggest tone.
paragraphs: A Persian miniature is a small painting made for a book. The painter uses flat areas of mineral colour (lapis from the mines of Badakhshan, vermilion, malachite green, turmeric yellow and burnished gold leaf), draws fine ink outlines, and does not cast shadows. Space is made by stacking things up the page, and meadows are pricked with tufts of grass and small flowers. A frame of gold rules, a blue band with gold teardrops and a ground of ivory paper surrounds the page. The program follows the same recipe.

The picture is blurred (simplify × 1.1 px), made 25% more saturated, and snapped to one of nine pigments by the redmean distance used on the Truck Art page. Specks are removed by a majority filter, run twice over a 5 × 5 window. Outlines in dark brown ink are drawn where the colour index changes, with a strength of 0.8 × the ink slider. There are no shadows, but the painter’s trick for depth is fine parallel hatching, and the program uses it where the picture is dark: hatch lines every 3.1 px, at a slant, darken the colour by up to 34%. Tufts of grass (on green and turquoise, and sometimes elsewhere) and flecks of gold are scattered on a jittered grid of 30 px wherever there is no outline. The frame is built from ivory, a lapis band, gold rules, a red hairline and gold teardrops spaced 0.55 m apart, where m is the frame width.

equations.note: Brightness of the flat colour. The second term is the hatching: η is the hatching slider, and it only applies where the tone t is below 0.42.
Ink outline with strength λ, where ι is the ink slider (0 to 1) and C_ink is the dark brown (42, 26, 16).
Size and opacity of a fleck of gold: ξ is a random number and γ the gold slider.
The frame. It is dropped when m is under 8 px.

presets.text: Strong gold and a heavy frame make an illuminated page.
Fine ink lines with little hatching look crisp and calligraphic.
Heavy simplification gives bold flat colour.
